newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda president makes bricks in housing drive.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda president makes bricks in housing drive.

text.p: Rwanda's president made mud bricks on Thursday at the launch of a house-building programme for more than half a million returning refugees to help bridge the rift of genocide.

Sweating and wearing wellington boots, President Pasteur Bizimungu and almost the entire Rwandan cabinet spent two hours making bricks at 18 sites around the Rwandan capital Kigali to lead thousands at the start of the housing campaign.

Bizimungu told reporters the programme would help end the housing crisis and foster solidarity in a society split by genocide in 1994 in which up to a million ethnic Tutsis and Hutu moderates were killed by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
"All catergories of people are here," the Hutu president said.

"If vulnerable groups can accept to collaborate and build for everybody that means a philosophy has been accepted by everyone that we are all human beings and all need a roof over our heads," he added.
"I am getting my hands dirty because I am a member of this community and I have to participate in national solidarity," he said, before continuing work on 50 large bricks he had made.
The U.S. army estimates 630,000 Rwandan Hutus returned home between November 15 and 19 after being dislodged from camps in eastern Zaire by fighting between Zairean rebels and Zairean troops.

In the Tanzanian capial Dar es Salaam, the U.N. refugee agency and the Tanzanian government told more than half a million Rwandan refugees in Tanzania on Thursday they should return home by the end of December, a U.N. official said.
Two million Hutus, many of them fearing reprisals for the mass slaughter, had fled to Zaire, Tanzania and Burundi.
The returnees are competing for housing with 800,000 Tutsis who came home mainly from Uganda in 1994 after a civil war and genocide which the government estimates destroyed some 200,000 houses.
Soldiers, school children, returning Hutu refugees and Tutsi genocide survivors laboured with hoes and bare hands at the sites and many said they would return to continue building.
"I am completely in favour of this project because people need places to live," said Constantine Makoma, 30.
Makoma, a Tutsi, said he returned to Rwanda from Uganda and moved into a house abondoned by a Hutu who fled to Zaire.

"When I came back I found someone else living in my house but I've talked to the person and they have agreed to move out. That is why I am here," said Leanord Nyandwi, a Hutu who said he returned last week.
The cabinet's presence on Thursday was a bid for publicity for the house-building campaign but witnesses noted a high degree of public enthusiasm for the project and reconciliation.

The government has given Rwandans living in houses owned by Hutu refugees who have returned 15 days to move out and says the deadline could give up to 100,000 Hutu families the chance to take back their property.
Major Rose Kabuye, the prefect of Kigali, said about 15,000 Hutus returned to Kigali from camps in eastern Zaire last month and the government intended to build 10,000 new houses for them.
Funding would come from government, from local contributions and from international donors, according to Patrick Mazimhaka, minister for rehabilitation and social integration.
The government has appealed to the international community for up to $700 million to help returnees.
